passages.t: Twenty-three years unheard, and seventy years for Babylon
passages.happening:
The word came to Jeremiah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, the first year of Nebuchadnezzar (verse 1). For twenty-three years, from Josiah's thirteenth year, Jeremiah has spoken the LORD's word again and again, and they have not listened (verse 3). God sent all his servants the prophets, telling them to turn from their evil ways and not follow other gods (verses 4 to 6). But they did not listen (verse 7).

So God will summon the peoples of the north and send for ‘My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon’ (verse 9) against the land and the nations around it. He will take away the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of bride and bridegroom, the sound of the millstones and the light of the lamp (verse 10). ‘And this whole land will become a desolate wasteland, and these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years’ (verse 11).

‘But when seventy years are complete, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation’ (verse 12), and make it a desolation forever. Many nations and great kings will enslave the Babylonians in turn, and God will repay them for their deeds (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 lines up two reigns: the fourth year of Jehoiakim was the first of Nebuchadnezzar. That is 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar, then crown prince, crushed the Egyptian army at Carchemish on the Euphrates and became king when his father died. Carchemish settled that Babylon, not Egypt, would rule the region.

God calls Nebuchadnezzar his servant. It does not mean he worshiped the LORD. It means he was the tool God would use, as a king uses a servant, and the same chapter says Babylon would be judged in its turn.

Verse 10 lists the sounds of an ordinary town: wedding songs, the grinding of millstones each morning as women made the day's flour, and oil lamps burning in houses at night. When they stop, no one is left to marry, eat or live.
passages.later: Daniel read this very prophecy, ‘that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years’ (Daniel 9:2). Chronicles says the land rested ‘until seventy years were completed, in fulfillment of the word of the LORD through Jeremiah’ (2 Chronicles 36:21).
passages.hard:
Did the seventy years actually add up, and how should the number be read?

Believing readers have answered in more than one way. Some take the number as exact and find a seventy-year span: from Babylon's rise around 609 to 605 BC to its fall in 539 BC, or from the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC to its rebuilding around 516 BC. Both come close, and the Bible itself seems to use both (Ezra 1:1 ties it to Cyrus; Zechariah 1:12 to the ruined temple). Others read seventy as a round number for a lifetime, the span of years in Psalm 90:10, meaning the exile would outlast the generation that caused it.

Either way, the limit matters most. The prophecy told the exiles not to expect a quick return, as the false prophets promised, and not to despair of any return at all. Daniel 9 later reads Jeremiah's seventy years and receives a vision of seventy weeks of years. These notes calculate no date from these numbers.
passages.asks: Jeremiah preached for twenty-three years with no one listening. Ask how you would keep going in that. And ask what it means for you that even a long judgment has a limit God has set.

passages.t: The cup of wrath for the nations
passages.happening:
God tells Jeremiah, “Take from My hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink from it” (verse 15). They will drink and stagger because of the sword God sends (verse 16). Jeremiah takes the cup and makes the nations drink (verse 17): Jerusalem and Judah first (verse 18), then Egypt, the Philistines, Edom, Moab and Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, the desert peoples, Elam and Media, all the kings of the north, and last the king of Sheshach (verses 19 to 26).

If they refuse the cup, they must drink anyway (verse 28). ‘For behold, I am beginning to bring disaster on the city that bears My Name, so how could you possibly go unpunished?’ (verse 29).

The LORD will roar from on high and bring a charge against the nations (verses 30 and 31). Disaster spreads from nation to nation like a storm (verse 32). The shepherds, the leaders of the flock, are told to wail, for there is no escape (verses 34 and 35). He has left his den like a lion, and the land is desolate (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The cup was a familiar picture in Israel's poetry. God gives each person a cup, a portion to drink, and the cup of wrath makes the drinker stagger like a drunk man. Judgment is pictured as forced drunkenness.

The list moves outward from Jerusalem across the known world: Egypt to the south, the Philistine cities on the coast, the peoples east of the Jordan, the Phoenician ports, the Arabian tribes, and Elam and Media far to the east. Sheshach is a coded name for Babylon, formed by swapping the letters of the alphabet from the end, so Babylon drinks last.

Verse 29 is the hinge. Judgment begins at the city that bears God's name. If God does not spare his own city, no nation can expect to escape.

The Greek translation of Jeremiah places the oracles against the nations after verse 13, in a different order. These chapters are poetry of judgment on ancient powers. They draw no line to any nation of the present day.
passages.later: Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem as one who has ‘drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury’ (Isaiah 51:17). Peter writes, ‘it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God’ (1 Peter 4:17).
passages.asks: Judgment begins with the city that bears God's name. Ask what it means for those who belong to God to be judged first. And ask whether you are quicker to see God's judgment on others than on yourself.
